The verb garnish has two entirely separate meanings — one used in everyday cooking and food, and one used in law and finance. They share the same word but mean completely different things, so it's important to know both.
Meaning 1: To decorate or add finishing touches to food or drink

When you garnish something in the context of cooking, you add a small item to a dish or drink — not as a main ingredient, but to make it look more appealing, more elegant, or to add a small burst of flavor or color right before it's served.

Think of it as the final touch a chef gives to a plate before it goes to the table.

Examples:

  • She garnished the pasta with fresh basil leaves and a drizzle of olive oil.
  • The bartender garnished the cocktail with a slice of lime and a mint sprig.
  • The soup was garnished with a swirl of cream and a sprinkle of paprika.

The item you add — the basil, the lime slice, the cream — is called a garnish (the noun form of the same word). Typical garnishes include fresh herbs (parsley, cilantro, mint), citrus slices or wedges, edible flowers, sauces drizzled on top, grated cheese, toasted nuts, whipped cream, chocolate shavings, or even just a simple dusting of a spice.

Important nuance: A garnish is almost always optional — the dish is already complete without it. It's added purely for presentation and a small sensory enhancement, not as a core component of the recipe. This is what distinguishes garnishing from regular cooking. If you're adding a primary ingredient midway through cooking, that's not garnishing. Garnishing happens at the end, when the food is essentially ready, and the purpose is finishing, not building.

You can also occasionally see this word used outside food — to garnish a room or a piece of writing means to decorate or embellish it. But this usage is rare and slightly old-fashioned. In modern everyday language, you'll almost always encounter this meaning in a food or drink context.
Meaning 2: To legally seize or withhold someone's money to pay a debt

This meaning lives in the world of law and finance, and it is completely unrelated to food. To garnish someone's wages, salary, or bank account means that a court or government authority legally orders that a portion of their money be taken — before it even reaches the person — and given directly to someone they owe money to.

In other words, if you owe money and refuse to pay (or can't), a court can step in and say: "We will take the money directly from your paycheck or bank account and hand it to your creditor." This process is called garnishment (noun), or more specifically, wage garnishment or bank garnishment.

Examples:

  • The court ordered the company to garnish 20% of his wages until the debt was paid off.
  • Because she had unpaid student loans in default, the government began to garnish her salary.
  • If you don't settle the judgment, the creditor can petition the court to garnish your bank account.

Notice who does what here: the court issues the order; the employer (or bank) is legally required to comply; and the creditor (the person or organization owed money) receives the withheld funds. The person whose money is being taken is called the debtor.

This form of garnishing is involuntary — the debtor doesn't choose it. It's a legal enforcement tool used when someone has failed to repay a debt despite a court judgment. Common scenarios include unpaid taxes, defaulted loans, child support arrears, or credit card debt that has gone to court.

The two meanings of garnish couldn't feel more different, so context will always make it clear which one is being used. If the sentence is about food, a plate, a dish, a drink, or a chef, it's the decorating meaning. If the sentence is about wages, salaries, courts, debt, creditors, or bank accounts, it's the legal seizure meaning.
Degree and strength of the word

In the food sense, garnish is a light word — it implies something small, delicate, and optional. You don't garnish with a main ingredient; you garnish with something subtle that enhances the whole.

In the legal sense, garnish is a forceful word — it implies something imposed against your will, a consequence of unresolved debt. It carries weight and seriousness.
Quick mental image to remember both

• Food: A chef places a sprig of mint on top of a dessert just before serving → garnishing the dish.
  • Legal: A court takes 15% of a worker's salary every month and hands it to a debt collector → garnishing the wages.

Both share the idea of something being taken from or added to something larger, but in radically different situations.
